Diagnosis includes biopsy of small bowel and confirmation of response to diet for most patients (). C
Diagnosis can alternatively be made with a positive endomysial antibody test and high titers of tissue transglutaminase. B

Patients with diabetes mellitus type 1, Down's syndrome, Turner's syndrome, IgA deficiency, and first- or second-degree relatives with celiac disease have an increased risk of having celiac disease. B
Avoid wheat, barley, and rye, which are gluten-containing grains. Lifelong strict adherence to a gluten-free diet significantly improves symptoms and reduces the risk of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. B
Nearly all patients will have the HLA genotypes DQ2 and/or DQ8, which can assist in cases where the diagnosis is uncertain. B

background.definition: Celiac disease is a chronic autoimmune disorder of small bowel malabsorption. It is characterized by small bowel damage that occurs upon exposure to ingested gluten in a genetically predisposed individual and clinical and histological improvement with withdrawal of gluten from the diet.

list.listitem: Estimates of the prevalence in the United States range from 0.4% to 1.0%.

In a study at a large health fair in Wyoming, 34 of 3850 persons tested positive for both serum tissue transglutaminase antibody and endomysial antibody. Three had a known diagnosis; of the other 31 who were offered small bowel biopsy, 18 agreed, and 17 had evidence of villous atrophy. Overall prevalence was therefore 0.8%.
There is an estimated worldwide prevalence of about 0.5% to 1% except in areas with low prevalence of gluten ingestion including Japan and Western Africa.

Celiac disease is seen in genetically predisposed individuals, with nearly all patients having the HLA genotypes DQ2 and DQ8. Those without these genotypes can be virtually excluded from having celiac disease.
Breast feeding during the introduction of gluten and increased duration of breast feeding have been associated with a decreased risk of developing celiac disease.

Although previous systematic reviews suggested that the timing of gluten introduction is not associated with the risk of developing celiac disease, an analysis of the open-label Enquiring About Tolerance (EAT) trial that randomized 1,303 exclusively breastfed infants to the introduction of gluten at 4 or 6 months of age found a reduced prevalence of celiac disease at 3 years in the earlier-introduction group (NNT = 72).

Celiac disease is an immune-mediated response to ingested gluten (wheat, barley, and rye), the indigestable gluen fragments lodge in the lamina priopria which leads to mucosal inflammation, small intestinal villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia to the small bowel.
This damage leads to a host of signs, symptoms, and complications, which manifest both locally and systemically.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force concluded that the evidence was insufficient to determine the balance of benefits and harms of screening in the general population and persons at increased risk. Therefore, screening asymptomatic individuals is not recommended. C

Screening adult relatives of patients with known celiac disease and assigning those who tested positive to a gluten-free diet reduced indigestion and reflux symptoms, but negatively affected social functioning. B
Introducing small amounts of dietary gluten at 16 to 24 weeks of age in high-risk infants did not reduce the incidence of celiac disease at age 3 years. B
Assess for nutritional deficiencies common in those with celiac disease, including folic acid, B12, fat-soluble vitamins, iron, and calcium. C
Consider periodic screening for osteoporosis with bone densitometry. C

For the general population (without known celiac disease), there is uncertainty whether gluten-reduced or gluten-free diet is effective in the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease or that it improves all-cause mortality. B

Celiac disease classically presents with bloating, flatulence or gas, chronic unexplained diarrhea, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, loss of appetite, and symptoms since childhood. B
Diagnosis includes biopsy of small bowel and confirmation of response to diet for most patients (). C

Diagnosis can alternatively be made with a positive endomysial antibody test and high titers of tissue transglutaminase. Serum IgA antiendomysial antibodies and antitissue transglutaminase are more sensitive and specific than antigliadin antibodies. B
The most common extraintestinal manifestations of celiac disease are undiagnosed iron-deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, autoimmune thyroid disease, and elevated liver enzymes. C

If serological screening is positive, a biopsy of the small bowel (beyond the second portion of the duodenum) showing characteristic mucosal changes is the current gold standard for confirming the diagnosis of celiac disease (), as well as response to gluten-free diet. C

Diagnosis may be made using the nonvalidated "four out of five" rule, which includes (1) typical signs and symptoms, (2) positive antibody testing, (3) HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 positivity, (4) intestinal damage on biopsy (eg, villous atrophy), and (5) resolution of symptoms with gluten-free diet. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease that may involve any part of the GI tract
Refers to the intestinal manifestations of Whipple's disease
Infection of small intestine by Actinomycete Tropheryma whippelii; extraintestinal manifestations more dramatic
Self-limited disease or identification of known pathogen
High prevalence, alternating constipation and diarrhea for most; ROME criteria
Finding of eosinophilic infiltrate on colonic biopsy
Positive hydrogen breath test confirms diagnosis
Symptoms suggestive of celiac disease but negative confirmatory tests; symptoms improve with gluten-reduced or gluten-free diet

list.listitem: There are 4 recognized presentations of celiac disease: classic, atypical, silent, and latent:
Classic celiac disease: GI manifestations with positive antibody markers, typical small bowel biopsy results, and resolution with a gluten-free diet.
Atypical celiac disease: predominantly extraintestinal manifestations with positive antibody markers, typical small bowel biopsy results, and resolution with a gluten-free diet.

Silent celiac disease: asymptomatic individuals screened for various reasons (including high-risk individuals) with positive antibody markers and typical small bowel biopsy results (possibly found on biopsy for other reasons).
Latent celiac disease: asymptomatic individuals with positive antibody markers but no evidence of disease on small bowel biopsy.

Celiac disease can present in many different ways. In classic celiac disease, GI manifestations (bloating, flatulence/gas, chronic unexplained diarrhea, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, loss of appetite, and symptoms since childhood) predominate, with no one or two features guiding suspicions more than the others.

In a study of 2568 primary care patients, 976 had anemia, family history, or at least 1 GI symptom and were evaluated for celiac disease. The researchers found that between 1% and 2% had a final diagnosis of celiac disease.
Consider ruling out celiac disease in patients suspected of IBS given its prevalence (i.e., 6% pooled seroprevalence and 2% pooled biopsy-proven prevalence among patients with IBS).
Vitamin D deficiency with hypocalcemia, vitamin K deficiency, and folate deficiency have been seen with the malabsorptive effects of the GI manifestations of celiac disease.

Extraintestinal manifestations of celiac disease are common. Dermatitis herpetiformis, which is the cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease, is an intensely pruritic papulovesicular rash that usually appears on the extensor surfaces of the extremities, buttocks, trunk, neck, and scalp.

Patients with celiac disease are at increased risk of osteoporosis, and fractures are increased (OR 3.5; 1.8-7.2). There may be an association with infertility (2.7% of patients with unexplained infertility have evidence of subclinical celiac disease).

Other symptoms sometimes seen in patients with celiac disease are weight loss, loss of appetite, chronic fatigue, ataxia, idiopathic epilepsy, psychosis, and migraines. There may be associated peripheral neuropathy involving the peripheral small fibres and ganglions

In the pediatric population, infants and young children most commonly present with diarrhea, failure to thrive, and abdominal distention. Older children and adolescents may present with delayed puberty, short stature, neurologic symptoms, or anemia.
Interestingly not all patients present malnourished, about 40% may be overweight or obese at the time of diagnosis

Consider celiac disease in the differential diagnosis of patients with unexplained anemia, infertility, autoimmune disease including comorbid thyroid disease, or abnormal bone density. Liver disease and elevated liver function tests of unknown origin have also been associated with celiac disease and may resolve with a gluten-free diet. In 1 report, 6.4% of patients with autoimmune hepatitis had celiac disease.

Patients suspected of having celiac disease should undergo serologic testing with IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase and/or IgA antiendomysial antibody tests. These tests have taken the place of antigliadin antibodies due to their high sensitivity and specificity..

ACG guidelines (2023) recommend biopsy to confirm the diagnosis, but acknowledge that high titers for both IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase and IgA antiendomysial antibody tests are a reliable alternative.
A biopsy of the skin demonstrating dermatitis herpetiformis (granular deposits of IgA by immunofluorescence) in a patient with positive serology is sufficient to diagnose celiac disease.

Otherwise, patients with abnormal serology should undergo biopsy of the small bowel from the second portion of the duodenum or beyond. Celiac patients will have intestinal biopsies that show atrophy of the small intestinal villi, deepening of the crypts, and infiltration of the lamina propria and intraepithelial compartments with chronic inflammatory cells.

In those patients with positive serology and the characteristic mucosal changes of celiac disease on biopsy, a gluten-free diet should be initiated. Definitive diagnosis is made when there is a resolution of symptoms on a gluten-free diet. A confirmatory biopsy showing resolution of mucosal changes is no longer recommended.
If the diagnosis is uncertain, consider genetic markers of the HLA haplotypes DQ2 and/or DQ8; either of them is present in nearly 100% of celiac patients.

IgA deficiency is 10 to 15 times more prevalent in celiac patients and serum total IgA levels must be checked as part of the work up. If the IgA antiendomysial and IgA antitissue transglutaminase antibodies are negative in the presence of IgA deficiency, test for the IgG version of these markers.
Suspect celiac disease in patients with chronic GI symptoms.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation and treatment.
Avoid wheat, barley, and rye; these are the gluten-containing grains. Lifelong strict adherence of a gluten-free diet significantly improves symptoms and reduces the risk of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. B
All serologic testing and biopsies must be completed before starting gluten restriction. C
Recommend a multivitamin and appropriate supplements to correct for deficiencies often seen with malabsorptive effects of the disease. C
Consider referral to dietitician experienced in celiac disease. C
People initially diagnosed with celiac disease should receive a multivitamin and appropriate supplements to correct for deficiencies often seen with malabsorptive effects of the disease.

In celiac disease that is refractory to a gluten-free diet, rule out ongoing inadvertent gluten ingestion in diet and medications. Corticosteroids and/or immunosuppressants may be beneficial in the acute setting, but their long-term benefits are uncertain.
Immunosuppressants may promote the progression of lymphoma in celiac patients.
There is insufficient evidence that probiotics improve symptoms or quality of life.
Avoid wheat, barley, and rye; these are the gluten-containing grains. Nutrition counseling is recommended. Diet is very challenging because gluten is contained in many processed foods.
Patients wanted to be 66% sure of the diagnosis before embarking on a gluten free diet if symptomatic, and 90% sure if asymptomatic based on a systematic review.

Introduction of gluten through cereals before or after 4 to 6 months has been shown to increase the risk of developing celiac disease in some studies,although a systematic review of mostly observational studies found that these associations disappeared after controlling for breastfeeding and type of flour.Experts recommending introducing gluten between 4 and 6 months.

Dermatitis herpetiformis (an intensely pruritic papulovesicular rash that usually appears on the extensor surfaces of the buttocks, extremities, trunk, neck, and scalp) resolves with a gluten-free diet.
Gluten consumption of up to 30 mg/day (equal to a diet containing 300 g of flour/day with 100 ppm) showed no effect on mucosal histology.

Pure oats can safely be consumed by patients with celiac disease. A small amount of gluten contamination is common in rice, corn, and oat products but generally does not reach the threshold of mucosal damage. When initially instituting a gluten-free diet, wheat, barely, rye, as well as oats should be avoided. Once this diet has been well established, patients may safely introduce oats but should stop if they develop symptoms.

Low fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols (FODMAP) gluten-free diet may be helpful in patients with biopsy-proven celiac disease who have persistent symptoms despite adherence to gluten-free diet. It is also effective for patients with irritable bowel syndrome.
Celiac disease requires lifelong adherence to a gluten-free diet or its manifestations will return.
Complications are usually uncommon and occur in about 2% of those diagnosed with the condition

Some patients may develop refractory celiac disease which is defined as the persistence or reoccurence of symptoms despite the adherence to a gluten-free diet for a year and the absence of a malignancy such as enteropathy associated lymphoma.

Refractory celiac disease can progress to enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma or ulcerative jejunitis. Double-balloon enteroscopy is an efficient method for detecting or excluding these complications.
Celiac patients who strictly adhere to a gluten-free diet have survival rates (at 5 years follow-up) equal to the general population in Finland. B

Celiac patients who maintain a normal diet, only adhere to a reduced gluten diet, or have refractory disease have an increase increased all-cause mortality and increased incidence in intestinal lymphoma and cancers of the mouth, pharynx, and esophagus. B

At 3 to 6 months on a gluten-free diet, approximately half of children will be negative for antitissue transglutaminase antibodies. This can be helpful in determining compliance with a gluten-free diet. C

Patients with celiac disease are at an increased risk of a number of cancers. Adenocarcinoma of the small intestines (usually of the jejunum) and cancers of the mouth, pharynx, and esophagus are more prevalent in celiac patients.
Celiac patients are at increased risk of non-Hodgkin's lymphomas and enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphomas, with a prognosis of 20% survival over 30 months in the latter.
Symptom resolution is generally excellent for those who can adhere to strict diet with seroconversion approaching 95% at 5 year follow up.
Intestinal mucosal healing may take up to 3 years.
Patients who adhere to a strict gluten-free diet do not have an increased risk of non-Hodgkin's lymphomas.
Consider monitoring celiac patients for osteoporosis.
The persistence of antiendomysial antibodies or antitissue transglutaminase antibodies after 1 year of a gluten-free diet suggests poor compliance.
Antiendomysial and antitissue transglutaminase antibodies have a low sensitivity for minor dietary indiscretions.
Approximately 19% of patients with celiac disease are over the age of 60 years. These patients present most often with classic signs of malabsorption and GI symptoms.
Thrombocytosis has been reported as the presenting sign of celiac disease in the elderly, which resolves with a gluten-free diet.
Celiac disease may develop during pregnancy or postpartum and should be considered especially with severe iron-deficiency anemia.
Children with celiac disease have a 3-fold increased risk of long-term mortality (OR 3.3; 95% CI, 2.1-5.1) compared with a 40% increase (OR 1.4; 95% CI, 1.2-1.6) in adult celiac patients.

Infants and young children generally present with diarrhea, abdominal distention, and failure to thrive. Older children and adolescents often present with short stature, neurological symptoms, or anemia.

Order IgA tissue transglutaminase and/or IgA antiendomysial antibody.
Celiac disease confirmed. Continue diet, evaluate for malabsorption, consider multivitamins as needed.
Small bowel biopsy (second portion of duodenum or beyond).
Celiac disease likely; symptoms improve on gluten-free diet?
Assess dietary compliance; if patient is compliant, consider other causes for symptoms.
Celiac disease unlikely; consider repeat biopsy of small bowel if serology had been abnormal; biopsy skin if dermatitis herpetiformis suspected clinically.
